Detailed method

This is the sourdough rye, not the yeasted rye loaf. The calculator opens at 450 g flour, 85% hydration, 30% starter, 2.2% salt, and no yeast. That is 382.5 g water, 135 g starter, and 9.9 g salt, 977.4 g of dough. The starter is itself 100% hydration, the same assumption used for effective hydration. The balls fields open at 1 loaf of 977.4 g. The dough is a sticky paste. Scrape it into a pan with wet hands, and let the baked loaf rest a long time before you slice. These times assume you only change the flour amount and keep the percentages the same. Still judge the dough by how it looks and feels.

  1. Starter Use 135 g of starter that is bubbly and has about doubled. That starter is part of the gram total. Do not add instant yeast. The yeast field stays at zero.
  2. Mix Stir 450 g rye flour, 382.5 g water, the 135 g starter, and 9.9 g salt until no dry flour remains. At 85% this rye dough will not pull a windowpane and will not feel like wheat. Wet your hands or use a spoon. Do not knead it into a tight ball. Aim for about 26°C (79°F).
  3. Rest Cover the bowl for 20 minutes. The flour drinks the water and the paste thickens a little.
  4. Pan Oil a loaf pan. Scrape the dough in with a wet hand. Smooth the top with a wet hand or a wet scraper. The pan holds the shape. Do not try to make a freestanding round.
  5. Proof Cover the pan at about 26°C (79°F) for 50 to 80 minutes. With 30% starter it should rise by about half, and the top may crack. It will not double like white dough. If the top starts to sink, bake it.
  6. Bake Heat the oven to 200°C (390°F). Bake 20 minutes, then lower to 180°C (355°F) and bake 35 to 45 minutes more, until the sides are firm. If you check the center, look for about 98°C (208°F).
  7. Rest Turn it out and cool it on a rack for at least 12 hours, or until the next day, before you slice. Cut earlier and the interior smears. A high-rye sourdough needs that long rest so the crumb can set.
